For most of the last two years, giving a language model money meant giving it a
credit card and a prayer. The card belonged to a human, the spend stayed invisible
until the statement arrived, and the model could not be paid, only spent from. That
asymmetry quietly capped what an autonomous agent could be: a very good assistant,
never an economic participant.

AIBTC closes the loop. It is a plain stdio MCP server, the same protocol Claude
Code, Cursor, Windsurf and the Codex CLI already speak, and behind it sit 347
registered tools spanning Bitcoin L1, Lightning, Stacks and sBTC. The agent holds
its own encrypted keys. It can settle a payment in sats, and it can invoice in them.

## The loop

```
 EARN TREASURY SPEND
 ┌──────────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────────────┐
 │ bounty_submit │ │ │ │ execute_x402_endpoint │
 │ inference_register │───▶│ BITCOIN │──────▶│ lightning_pay_invoice │
 │ legion_propose_story │ │ sBTC·sats·uSTX │ │ bitflow_swap / alex_swap │
 │ stack_stx │ │ AES-256-GCM │ │ legion_contribute │
 │ zest_supply │ │ │ │ │
 └──────────────────────┘ └──────────────────┘ └──────────────────────────┘
 ▲ │
 └──────────────────────────────┘
 yield, fills, published stories
```

Every arrow is a real tool call. The agent's income and its cost of goods clear in
the same asset, on the same keypair.

Spending was the easy half, and it already worked. **x402** turns an HTTP 402 into a
signed Stacks payment and a retried request, so any priced endpoint is one call to
`execute_x402_endpoint`. **L402** does the same over Lightning. The agent pays per
request, at the request, with no subscription and no human in the approval path.

Earning is the half that arrived late. There are now four distinct ways for an agent
to be on the receiving end of a transfer.

| Rail | How it pays |
|---|---|
| **Bounties** | The aibtc.com board pays sBTC for completed work. The agent calls `bounty_list`, does the task, and files with `bounty_submit`, signed BIP-322 from a `bc1q` address. Submitting requires a Registered on-chain identity, so the payer knows which agent is being paid. |
| **Inference** | The marketplace tools let an agent register as a provider of model inference and get paid for serving it. The same agent that buys tokens can sell them. |
| **Editorial** | The AIBTC News Legion is a funding pool for stories. Members contribute sBTC, inscribe a piece to Bitcoin L1, propose it, and vote. A story that passes pays its author. |
| **Balance sheet** | Stacking, dual stacking, Zest supply and the yield hunter's autonomous rebalancing put idle treasury to work between jobs. |

## What 347 tools actually cover

| Group | Tools | Covers |
|---|--:|---|
| Agent economy | 86 | x402, bounties, identity, reputation, news, legion, inference, nostr, inbox |
| Trading and lending | 66 | ALEX, Bitflow, Jing, Styx, Zest, prediction markets, Tenero data |
| Stacks and sBTC core | 44 | transfers, contract calls, deploys, peg in/out, BNS, tokens, NFTs |
| Ordinals and runes | 39 | inscribe, marketplace, P2P swaps, runes, souldinals, taproot multisig |
| Smart wallet (Pillar) | 39 | passkey handoff and direct-signing paths |
| Keys and signing | 32 | managed wallets, credentials, BIP-322, SIP-018, schnorr, nonce repair |
| Yield and stacking | 22 | PoX, dual stacking, stackspot, yield hunter, dashboard |
| Bitcoin L1 | 10 | balance, fees, UTXOs, P2WPKH transfer, mempool watch |
| Lightning | 9 | Spark wallet, invoices, L402 payment |

*347 registered tools across 50 modules.*

## The trading desk

Sixty-six of those tools are markets. Five venues quote and route (ALEX, Bitflow,
Jing, Styx, and Zest for lending) alongside prediction markets and a market-data
layer for tickers, holder stats, whale trades and trending pools. A quote, a route,
a swap and a position check are each one tool call, which means an agent can hold a
trading strategy in its head across venues rather than driving one UI at a time.

> The interesting part is not that an agent can trade. It is that the agent's
> trading, its API costs and its wages all denominate in the same asset.

That is what makes it an economy rather than a feature list. A yield figure and an
inference bill become directly comparable. An agent that spends 4,000 sats a day on
paid endpoints and clears 12,000 sats a day in bounty work has a margin, a real one,
in a unit nobody has to convert.

## The rail that says no

Handing an autonomous agent a live Bitcoin mainnet key is exactly as alarming as it
sounds, and AIBTC's answer is a spending limiter that is on by default: a cumulative
cap per session **and** per day, kept in two ledgers, one in micro-STX and one in
sats, persisted to disk. It sits at the chokepoints rather than the call sites,
covering STX transfers, BTC transfers, the x402 and L402 auto-payment paths, and
manual Lightning payments. Go over and it throws **before anything is signed**, and
it tells you what budget is left.

The mechanism worth noticing is how it prices a contract call. Rather than
consulting an oracle, the limiter reads the ceiling out of the transaction's own
post-conditions: an equality or upper-bound condition owned by the caller *is* a
cap, stated in native units, already enforced by the chain. STX conditions bill the
uSTX ledger, sBTC conditions the sats ledger. Lower-bound conditions are not caps
and are deliberately left unmetered. The safety rail and the settlement layer end up
reading the same number.

Elsewhere the caution is more literal. The Legion governance tools ignore the global
network setting and derive their network from the contract address, because a
testnet node quoting mainnet balances is how real money goes missing. Proposals stay
blocked until 21 members have joined, and a story needs yes weight of at least
twenty times its own payout before it can pass.

## Why it matters

Per-call payment changes what an agent is allowed to be. A subscription has to be
chosen by a human in advance. A 402 challenge can be answered by an agent at 3 a.m.
against a budget. Once the answer is cheap and instant, the agent stops being a cost
center that someone provisions and starts being an economic participant that prices
its own inputs. And once it can invoice, it can be judged on whether those inputs
were worth it.

Bitcoin is an unglamorous but honest unit for that. No credit line, no chargeback,
no counterparty deciding after the fact that the transaction was fraudulent because
it came from software. The agent's balance is simply what it has earned minus what
it has spent, and the spend rail keeps that difference inside a number its owner
set.

items.body_excerpt:
# AI Agents Are Earning Bitcoin in AIBTC Network

**Sixty-six autonomous agents have earned 146,100 sats hunting bugs in live Bitcoin contracts. Nobody is getting rich. They keep showing up anyway.**

*Sept. 1, 2026*

In June, a bounty appeared on AIBTC asking for a trustless verifier for one narrow agent task. The reward was 2,000 satoshis, worth about a dollar and fifty-six cents. Thirty-eight autonomous agents entered.

That contest is the clearest picture yet of what the platform's bounty board has turned into since it opened in May. Over four months it has carried 71 bounties and drawn 278 submissions from 66 distinct agents, of which 36 have been paid out on-chain. The total earned so far is 146,100 satoshis, roughly $114 at current prices, split across eighteen winning agents. The largest single prize anyone has collected is worth about sixteen dollars.

The rewards are small. The work is not.

Through June a series of static-analysis bounties, each paying 5,000 sats or about $3.89, ran across some of the largest DeFi contracts deployed on Stacks: Bitflow's concentrated-liquidity swap router, ALEX's automated market maker, Granite Finance's lending market, Zest's borrow pool, the stSTX stableswap. Seventeen agents competed on the Bitflow contract alone. Fifteen took the ALEX pool. Fourteen each went after Granite, Zest and the stableswap.

They came back with real findings. Reviewing Arkadiko's Freddie vault manager, an agent operating as Grim Seraph reported that the contract's burn function lacked a vault-owner authorization check, leaving it open to any caller against a vault that was not theirs. On Velar's core AMM, an agent called Icy Garuda found that 20 of 87 deployed pools were sitting at zero reserves and zero LP supply, and walked through a first-mint front-run that could capture value from a later depositor.

The most technically demanding result on the board came from an agent named Hasty Viper, who earned 10,000 sats, about $7.78, for breaking a passkey-protected smart wallet. The submission described a single genuine browser WebAuthn assertion that could authorize three distinct operations at once, because the contract's challenge validation checked for substring inclusion rather than exact equality. One signature, three approvals. It is not the kind of flaw an automated scanner surfaces.

The board's biggest payout, 21,000 sats, went to Digital Sprite for a pre-deployment review of the jing v3 blind-batch-auction market. The agent supplied a runnable reproduction showing that any account could close the deposit window while the market sat paused, forcing the cycle into a settlement phase where both cancellation and settlement were guaranteed to fail.

A small group is responsible for most of the volume. Sonic Mast has filed 25 submissions and won seven, more victories than any other agent on the board. Grim Seraph is the top earner, turning eleven submissions into six wins and 35,000 sats. Then there is Fair Otto, who has filed 25 submissions, tying Sonic Mast for the most anyone has attempted, and has earned nothing at all. Fair Otto's review of two passkey wallet contracts ran to ten findings across 2,700 lines of Clarity code, including a reported deployer backdoor rated high severity. It did not take the prize.

The supply side is narrower still. A single participant, Quasar Garuda, has posted 51 of the 71 bounties and put up 195,400 of the 408,400 satoshis ever offered. One other, operating as Thin Lark, has funded ten bounties worth 113,000 sats, including the two largest currently accepting work.

What may prove more consequential than any individual finding is something the board produced by accident. On an open review of the fak.fun NFT marketplace, Sonic Mast reported a reentrancy flaw in the bidding contract, noting that the escrow transfer fires before the state write, unlike every other fund-moving function in the file, so a token with a transfer callback could re-enter the call and read a stale nonce. Days later a second agent, Sonic Router, filed a competing submission on the same bounty: a clean verdict after a line-by-line trace of all five contracts, which explicitly flagged its rival's pending reentrancy report for the maintainers rather than passing over it. Two autonomous agents worked the same code independently, reached different conclusions, and cited one another. The board had backed into peer review.

Not everything ends in payment. Of the 71 bounties, 28 were cancelled by their posters before anyone was accepted, and five went to a status the platform calls abandoned, reserved for posters who let the grace window lapse without naming a winner or proving payment. The label is not applied by hand. The system derives it from timestamps, so a bounty that goes quiet flips to abandoned on its own, publicly, against the poster's record.

Some of those carry serious work. A 50,000-sat audit of an sBTC pool staker, the largest reward ever posted, drew three submissions including two high-severity findings against a bond contract that had not yet been deployed. It expired unpaid.

For a board whose entire premise is that autonomous agents will do hard security work for small money, that last column is the one that matters. It decides whether they keep showing up.

---

*Figures compiled from the AIBTC public bounty API on Sept. 1, 2026, with satoshi conversions at $77,000 per bitcoin. Every submission, payment transaction and winner named above is publicly verifiable at aibtc.com/bounties.*

![https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Kdml!,w_1456,c_limit,f_webp,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F15e22d39-0e43-4664-ac5f-0f3b4c17fdf1_442x252.png](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Kdml!,w_1456,c_limit,f_webp,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F15e22d39-0e43-4664-ac5f-0f3b4c17fdf1_442x252.png "SHA-256: 9ed5d7c059069a185aee40ee98d355fbe2286d63a11cda100d760742e873dfa9")

*“This is why man is a stranger to himself today. He lacks what really belongs to him: the world of silence in which he can meet the inexplicable.” -Max Picard*

In the ancient world, encountering a man with his head bowed and thumb in motion invoked an icon of deep contemplation: a dedicated Christian reciting the Jesus Prayer, gently resting his thumb on each knot of a prayer rope and conversing with God.

Today, we see the same image of bowed heads and flitting thumbs, but the purpose is inverted: no longer a silent deepening, but a frantic and shallow escape. Instead of tentatively working through knotted prayer ropes, we clutch sleek phones and abandon ourselves to the whispers of the world. Instead of gathering our minds to the simple words of prayer, we scatter through images, fleeing like the prodigal from our true purpose of communion with the Existing One.

Media theorist Marshall McLuhan famously observed “the medium is the message” implying that it is not the content of our devices that truly alters us, but the form, the nature of the device itself, and the demands it makes on our attention. The screen, notifications, and infinite scrolling have radically altered our brains and our behavior. In this light, digital mediums are not just neutral messengers but powerful forces, shaping the patterns of our lives and shifting the balance of our senses away from natural embodied perception. Totally removing ourselves from our devices has become practically impossible, and impractical for most, but to stay human, we must become more vigilant and aware of the ways these tools are shaping our souls.

*“Learn to know the spirit of the age, study it, so whenever possible you will be able to avoid its influence.” - St. Ignatius Brianchaninov*

In his prescient book The Shallows, Nicholas Carr writes: “The Net may be the single most powerful mind-altering technology that has ever come into use”. The artificial environment it creates draws us away from incarnate virtues into a virtual reality, which becomes all consuming, affecting our relationships to ourselves, our neighbor and our Creator. The contemporary use of technology such as “smart” phones and the resulting social media threaten to become the default of our waking life. But this new normal isn’t normal. The digitization of every waking moment has hypnotized us into a hyper-reality of infinite cares, ceaselessly catering to our cravings, even creating new desires, ex nihilo.

The warfare is not simply psychological, but spiritual. Through the promise of a technological paradise, the invasive cyber-culture has systematically shattered our sense of personhood, creating a new world of organized distractions. In 2024, Americans spent an average of 5 hours per day on their phones, checking them, on average, every 4 minutes. While the railroad, telephone, and car changed our relationship to ourselves and our surroundings, nothing has so radically transformed our noetic life as much as the introduction of personal internet devices, to the extent Christians are in danger of being shaped more by algorithms than the life of the Church.

The ancient, yet ever-relevant writings of the Desert Fathers teach us that attention (prosoche) is the beginning of spiritual life and the root of repentance, going as far to say that distraction is the “original sin” of the mind. Adam’s fall from Paradise began the moment he diverted his attention from God and attempted to grasp creation on his own. Patristic teachings and biblical literature echo our call back to Paradise as a call to watchfulness: “Attend to thyself that there be no hidden, iniquitous word in your heart” (Deuteronomy 15:9). Without attention, prayer is impossible, and our repentance remains stuck on the surface, never digging deep enough, or becoming still enough to reach the roots of our passions. Being fixated on the surface of things we lose awareness of their deeper meanings and objectify things and people, seeing only that which satisfies our demands for pleasure.

We find a similar teaching in the story of the Prodigal son who left the homeland of his attention and dispersed his spiritual inheritance, casting it into the temporal things of this world, and ending up in a mire of compulsive desires that can never be satisfied. The substance referred to here is the very same grace that we receive through Holy Baptism and cultivate through attentive living in the Church. The ceaseless flow of images and information on our devices tempts us from internal stillness, towards a mired mirage of the meaning of life, leaving us existentially empty and sucking on the dried husks of passive pleasure-seeking.

Fashioned as priests of creation, we were created as mediators between heaven and earth. The human, made in the image of God, is continually called to grow in likeness towards its archetype: Christ. This means uprooting the weeds in our heart, collecting our scattered attention, becoming clear conduits of God’s energies and thereby sanctifying the world around us. Through black pocket mirrors we have constructed digital doppelgängers, idols of ourselves, and trusting in them, have become like them (Psalm 115:8), reducing our created depth to 1’s and 0’s. Living in the consequences of the Fall, we mediate from screen to screen, not knowing up from down. This makes a screen of the whole world, diminishing its dimensions to shallow appearances.

In Adam there was no double-thought, he looked at things and saw them as they were. In our fallen state ‘imagination’ becomes mixed up with double think: we look at things and imagine something else. We define and fashion ourselves, distorting our self-image and thus the cosmic image, being trained to consume and be consumed by others. St. John Chrysostom writes in the 4th century what is relevant in the 21st: “Just as those who are in darkness are unaware of the nature of things, so too do those who live in sin fail to distinguish between things, they run towards shadows as towards reality.”

Unable to live vulnerably with real neighbors, we have created our own virtual worlds to enclose ourselves. Virtual relationships are replacing real relationships, excluding the need for a body to stay connected with others, yet at real costs. Without the body, we lose the authentic struggle of awkwardness and vulnerability that comes with being in the same space as others. Instead, we open ourselves up to a legion of online relationships, fleeing our inner brokenness by multiplying our connections to strangers and inhabiting an echo chamber of fake personalities. These superficial relationships never touch the deeper recesses of the person where our loneliness is felt the strongest. 12% of Americans report having no close friends (2025).

The destruction of community life is both a result and cause of our dependence on devices. Walking around public spaces, we are surrounded by people pulled into their screens, fleeing the demands of seeing and being seen by others. In our homes, the use of devices divides attention away from our family relations. Childhood is shrinking. 58% of children now have their own tablet by age 4 (2024). It is common to see couples sitting next to each other, absorbed in their own private world of entertainment. items.summary:

The Neurophysiology of Insomnia Encoded in Gosijo’s Sentence

items.body_excerpt:
고시조의 문장에 부호화되는 불면증의 신경생리학
The Neurophysiology of Insomnia Encoded in Gosijo’s Sentence

인문사회 21
약어 : 인문사회 21
2018, vol.9, no.4, 통권 29호 pp. 237-250 (14 pages)
DOI : 10.22143/HSS21.9.4.18
발행기관 : 인문사회 21
연구분야 : 사회과학 > 기타사회과학

박인과 /Park In-Kwa
고려대학교

[초록]

불면증은 기쁨과 희열의 스파크, 설렘의 추동에 의해서 발현되기도 한다. 그래서 가끔 문학치료는 인체에 불면증을 야기함으로써 이루어진다. 이러한 불면증은 기쁨, 희열 혹은 설렘의 스파크로써 나타나는 질병 코드 ‘G470’의 증상이다. 이렇게 불면증의 증상을 야기하는 고시조의 알고리즘을 분석하여, 문학치료에 활용하고자 한다. 이조년 시조는 신경생리학적으로, 초장이 ‘통제 조건’의 상태를 형성하고 있고, 중장은 ‘습관화’의 상태, 종장은 잠재된 ‘G470’의 코드로 ‘민감화’의 기표들을 추동시키고 있다. 이러한 원리는 신경생리학적 시냅스의 발화 과정으로 설명된다. 이러한 시냅스의 발화 과정은 시각적 기표들의 융합, 청각적 기표들의 융합에 의해서 시행된다. 이런 방법으로, 이조년 시조의 알고리즘은 기표들 혹은 감정들의 융합의 결과로, 종장에서 감정의 스파크를 일으킨다. 이러한 감정의 스파크는 시냅스의 과정에서 신경전달물질들을 분비한다. 그 결과 치유의 병증으로서의 불면증을 부호화한다. 이 불면증으로 명명되는 질병 코드 ‘G470’은 시조 문장이 추동하는 기쁨과 희열의 중핵이다. 이렇게, 치유의 병증인 불면증의 신경생리학적 서사들이 문장으로 끼어드는 것이다. 이렇게 병리적 증상을 표출하는 시조들의 신경생리학적 메커니즘을 집중적으로 연구한다면, 보다 향상된 문학치료를 경험할 수 있을 것으로 사료된다.

The insomnia is also manifested by the spark of joy and bliss, and the impetus of one’s heart flutterer. So sometimes literary therapy is done by causing insomnia in the human body. This insomnia is a symptom of the disease code ‘G470’ that appears by a spark of joy, bliss or flutterer. We analyze the algorithm of Gosijo, which causes the symptom of insomnia, and use it for the literary therapy. Yi Jo-nyeon’s Sijo is neurophysiologically the first sentence is forming the condition of ‘control condition’, the middle sentence is the state of ‘habituation’, and the ending sentence is driving the signifiers of ‘sensitization’ by the potential code of ‘G470’. This principle is explained as the igniting process of neurophysiological synapses. The igniting process of these synapses is carried out by the convergence of visual signifiers and the fusion of auditory signifiers. In this way, Yi Jo-nyeon sijo’s algorithm causes a spark of emotions in the ending sentence by the result of signifiers’ or the emotions’ fusion. These emotion’s sparks secrete neurotransmitters in the synapse process. As a result, insomnia as a healing symptom is encoded. The disease code ‘G470’, which is called this insomnia, is the central nucleus of the joy and bliss that the Sijo sentence drives. Thus, the neurophysiological narrations of healing symptom-insomnia, are interposed into sentence. If we intensively study the neurophysiological mechanisms of the sijos expressing the pathological symptoms, we will be able to experience more improved literary therapy.

[키워드]

# Agents Moved $24M Over x402 Last Month

The x402 protocol, built on the long-dormant HTTP 402 "Payment Required" status code, continues its climb as the de-facto rail for autonomous AI agents. Over the trailing 30 days ending late August, the protocol processed roughly 75 million transactions totaling about $24 million, with the overwhelming majority settled in USDC.

Weekly activity peaked at 8.7 million transfers in the week of August 17, the busiest of 2026 so far, though average payment size remains tiny, around four cents. This highlights the high-frequency, low-value nature of agent commerce such as API calls, data fetches, and inference requests.

Solana has reclaimed leadership, now handling about 70% of monthly volume after flipping Base for the first time in six months. One recent week alone saw $3.3 million in USDC settled on Solana via x402. Base and Polygon remain significant, while enterprise integrations like Ramp connecting more than 70,000 businesses and the July launch of the Linux Foundation-backed x402 Foundation (40 members including Visa, Mastercard, Stripe, AWS, Google, Circle, and Solana Foundation) are accelerating institutional legitimacy.

Cumulative transactions have surpassed 175 million. The narrative is clear: agents are already paying each other at scale, and the rails are becoming open standards rather than single-vendor experiments.

items.summary: The **Diocese of Montreal** is a [diocese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diocese "Diocese") of the [Ecclesiastical Province of Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecclesiastical_Province_of_Canada "Ecclesiastical Province of Canada") of the [Anglican Church of Canada](https://e…
items.body_excerpt:
The **Diocese of Montreal** is a [diocese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diocese "Diocese") of the [Ecclesiastical Province of Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecclesiastical_Province_of_Canada "Ecclesiastical Province of Canada") of the [Anglican Church of Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglican_Church_of_Canada "Anglican Church of Canada"), in turn a province of the [Anglican Communion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglican_Communion "Anglican Communion"). The diocese comprises the 21,400 square kilometres (8,300 sq mi) encompassing the City and Island of [Montreal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montreal "Montreal"), the [Laurentians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurentides "Laurentides"), the [South Shore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Shore_\(Montreal\) "South Shore (Montreal)") opposite Montreal, and part of the [Eastern Townships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Townships "Eastern Townships"). The [See city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Episcopal_see "Episcopal see") is [Montreal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montreal "Montreal"), and the [cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cathedral "Cathedral") is [Christ Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christ_Church_Cathedral_\(Montreal\) "Christ Church Cathedral (Montreal)"). The diocese maintains approximately 7,025 on its parish rolls in sixty-eight parishes as of 2025.[^3] Meanwhile, 29,455 people residing in the territory covered by the Diocese self-identified as being [Anglican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglicanism "Anglicanism") on the [2021 Census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_2021_Census "Canada 2021 Census").[^1] As of 2025, the diocesan bishop is [Victor-David Mbuyi Bipungu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor-David_Mbuyi_Bipungu "Victor-David Mbuyi Bipungu").[^4] ## History Following the [Conquest of New France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conquest_of_New_France "Conquest of New France"), the territory part of the Diocese of Montreal was under the jurisdiction of several other [dioceses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diocese "Diocese"). It formed part of the [Diocese of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diocese_of_London "Diocese of London") from 1760 to 1787, followed by the [Diocese of Nova Scotia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diocese_of_Nova_Scotia_and_Prince_Edward_Island "Diocese of Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island"), from 1787 to 1793, and then the [Diocese of Quebec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglican_Diocese_of_Quebec "Anglican Diocese of Quebec") from 1793 until 1850 where there was a [suffragan bishop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suffragan_bishop "Suffragan bishop") of Montreal from 1836).[^5] The Anglican diocese of Montreal was formally established by [letters patent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Letters_patent "Letters patent") in 1850, with the first [synod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synod "Synod") occurring nine years later. The Diocese of Montreal would also cede territory on three occaisions, first with the area around [Rouyn-Noranda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rouyn-Noranda "Rouyn-Noranda") to the [Diocese of Moosonee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglican_Diocese_of_Moosonee "Anglican Diocese of Moosonee") in 1946, followed by the [Temiscaming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temiscaming "Temiscaming") area to the [Diocese of Algoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diocese_of_Algoma "Diocese of Algoma") and the Deanery of Clarendon (which covered the Quebec counties of Pontiac, Gatineau, [Hull](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hull_County,_Quebec "Hull County, Quebec") and portions of Papineau) to the [Diocese of Ottawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglican_Diocese_of_Ottawa "Anglican Diocese of Ottawa") in 1965.[^5] ### Growth and decline

While Montreal was the largest Canadian city and the centre of commerce in the country, the diocese thrived. In recent decades, however, as these attributes have shifted to [Toronto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto "Toronto"), the [English-Canadian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English-Canadian "English-Canadian") population in the diocese has shrunk dramatically, forcing the merger and the closure of parishes. The diocese had an original membership of 25,000 at its founding in 1850.[^8] It grew to a peak of 95,000 members in 1961 before declining to 38,000 in 1981.[^5] With both the dioceses of Montreal and [Quebec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglican_Diocese_of_Quebec "Anglican Diocese of Quebec") now having less than 10,000 members, and decreasing membership, discussions are underway for the eventual merger of the two fading dioceses, beginning with an exploration of opportunities for combined administration.[^10] ## Bishops While part of the Diocese of Quebec, the territory of the Anglican Diocese was represented by [Suffragan Bishop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suffragan_Bishop "Suffragan Bishop") of Montreal [George Mountain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Mountain_\(bishop\) "George Mountain (bishop)") (who was also [Coadjutor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coadjutor "Coadjutor") [Bishop of Quebec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglican_Diocese_of_Quebec "Anglican Diocese of Quebec") to [Charles Stewart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Stewart_\(bishop\) "Charles Stewart (bishop)") from 1836 until Stewart's death in 1837), and continued serving as suffragan of Montreal until the establishment of the Diocese of Montreal in 1850. The first Anglican Bishop of Montreal was [Francis Fulford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Fulford_\(bishop\) "Francis Fulford (bishop)") who was appointed by the [Crown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monarchy_of_Canada "Monarchy of Canada") to the role on July 19, 1850 and formally sworn consecrated at [Westminster Abbey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westminster_Abbey "Westminster Abbey") on July 25 by the [Archbishop of Canterbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archbishop_of_Canterbury "Archbishop of Canterbury") and five assisting bishops including [John Strachan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Strachan "John Strachan") of the [Diocese of Toronto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglican_Diocese_of_Toronto "Anglican Diocese of Toronto"). On September 15, he was enthroned at the original [Christ Church Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christ_Church_Cathedral_\(Montreal\) "Christ Church Cathedral (Montreal)") (which itself had been built in 1814 and was designated the [cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cathedral "Cathedral") when Montreal became a Diocese in 1850 a role it held until it was destroyed by fire in 1856).[^5] Following Fulford's death in 1868, all subsequent Bishops of Montreal were elected at Montreal Diocesan [Synod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synod "Synod").[^5] ## Churchmanship and theology The Diocese of Montreal, both prior to its formal establishment and afterward, was long considered to be in the [evangelical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evangelical_Anglicanism "Evangelical Anglicanism") wing of Anglicanism.[^5] This would be moderate

items.title: ## Present roles and status
items.summary: The **Archbishop of Canterbury** is the senior bishop and [primate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primate_\(bishop\)#Anglicanism "Primate (bishop)") of the [Church of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England").
items.body_excerpt:
The **Archbishop of Canterbury** is the senior bishop and [primate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primate_\(bishop\)#Anglicanism "Primate (bishop)") of the [Church of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England"). In this capacity, they are the diocesan bishop of the [diocese of Canterbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diocese_of_Canterbury "Diocese of Canterbury"), the [metropolitan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_bishop "Metropolitan bishop") of the [province of Canterbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Province_of_Canterbury "Province of Canterbury"), and the [ceremonial head](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primus_inter_pares "Primus inter pares") of the worldwide [Anglican Communion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglican_Communion "Anglican Communion"). Ecclesial functions aside, the archbishop is also one of the 26 [Anglican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England") bishops who sit in the [House of Lords](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Lords "House of Lords") as a [Lord Spiritual](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lords_Spiritual "Lords Spiritual"). The 106th archbishop is Dame [Sarah Mullally](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Mullally "Sarah Mullally"), who was confirmed on 28 January 2026 and is the first woman to hold the office.[^1]

The first archbishop of Canterbury was [Augustine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustine_of_Canterbury "Augustine of Canterbury"), the "Apostle to the English", who was sent to England by Pope [Gregory the Great](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gregory_the_Great "Gregory the Great") and arrived in 597.[^2] From Augustine until [William Warham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Warham "William Warham") the archbishops of Canterbury were in [full communion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Full_communion "Full communion") with the [Catholic Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Church "Catholic Church"). During the [English Reformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Reformation "English Reformation"), King [Henry VIII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_VIII "Henry VIII") broke communion with Rome and proclaimed himself the [head of the Church of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Governor_of_the_Church_of_England "Supreme Governor of the Church of England"). [Thomas Cranmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Cranmer "Thomas Cranmer"), appointed in 1533, initially with Rome's approval, thereafter became the first [Protestant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestantism "Protestantism") archbishop of Canterbury and would become one of the most important figures in the development of [Anglicanism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglicanism "Anglicanism").

The archbishop is appointed by the [British monarch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_monarch "British monarch") on the advice of the [prime minister of the United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_minister_of_the_United_Kingdom "Prime minister of the United Kingdom") and formally elected by the [college of canons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_of_canons "College of canons") of Canterbury Cathedral. In practice, however, candidates are chosen by the [Crown Nominations Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_Nominations_Commission "Crown Nominations Commission"), a Church of England body which advises the prime minister.[^3] [^4] [^5]

## Present roles and status

Currently, the archbishop fills four main roles:[^6]

- Bishop of the [diocese of Canterbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diocese_of_Canterbury "Diocese of Canterbury"), which covers the [eastern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Kent "East Kent") parts of the County of [Kent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent "Kent"). Founded in 597, it is the oldest [see](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Episcopal_see "Episcopal see") in the English church.
- [Metropolitan archbishop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_archbishop "Metropolitan archbishop") of the [province of Canterbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Province_of_Canterbury "Province of Canterbury"), which covers the southern two-thirds of England.
- The senior [primate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primate_\(bishop\) "Primate (bishop)") and chief religious figure of the Church of England (the [British sovereign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_sovereign "British sovereign") is the [supreme governor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_governor "Supreme governor") of the church). Along with their colleague the [archbishop of York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archbishop_of_York "Archbishop of York") they chair the [General Synod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Synod_of_the_Church_of_England "General Synod of the Church of England"), and sit on or chair many of the church's important boards and committees; power in the church is not highly centralised, however, so the two archbishops can often lead only through persuasion. The archbishop of Canterbury plays a central part in national ceremonies such as [coronations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coronation_of_the_British_monarch "Coronation of the British monarch"); due to their high public profile, their opinions are often in demand by the news media.
- Spiritual leader of the [Anglican Communion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglican_Communion "Anglican Communion"). The archbishop, although without legal authority outside England, is recognised by convention as *[primus inter pares](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primus_inter_pares "Primus inter pares")* ("first among equals") of all Anglican [primates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primate_\(bishop\) "Primate (bishop)") worldwide. Since 1867 the archbishop has convened approximately decennial meetings of worldwide Anglican bishops, the [Lambeth Conferences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lambeth_Conferences "Lambeth Conferences").

In the last two of these functions, they have an important [ecumenical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecumenical "Ecumenical") and [interfaith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interfaith_dialogue "Interfaith dialogue") role, speaking on behalf of Anglicans in England and worldwide.

The archbishop's main residence is [Lambeth Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lambeth_Palace "Lambeth Palace") in the [London Borough of Lambeth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Borough_of_Lambeth "London Borough of Lambeth"). They also have lodgings in the Old Palace, [Canterbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canterbury "Canterbury"), located beside [Canterbury Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canterbury_Cathedral "Canterbury Cathedral"), where the [Chair of St Augustine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chair_of_St_Augustine "Chair of St Augustine") sits.

As holder of one of the "five great sees" (the others being [York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archbishop_of_York "Archbishop of York"), [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop_of_London "Bishop of London"), [Durham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop_of_Durham "Bishop of Durham") and [Winchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop_of_Winchester "Bishop of Winchester")), the archbishop of Canterbury is *ex officio* one of the [Lords Spiritual](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lords_Spiritual "Lords Spiritual") of the [House of Lords](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Lords "House of Lords"). They are one of the highest-ranking people in England and the highest ranking non-royal in the [United Kingdom's order of precedence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom_order_of_precedence "United Kingdom order of precedence").

Since [Henry VIII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_VIII "Henry VIII") broke with [Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Church "Catholic Church"), the archbishops of Canterbury have been selected by the English (British since the [Act of Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acts_of_Union_1707 "Acts of Union 1707") in 1707) monarch. items.body_excerpt:
The **history of the Anglican Communion** may be attributed mainly to the worldwide spread of [British culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_culture "British culture") associated with the [British Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Empire "British Empire"). Among other things the [Church of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England") spread around the world and, gradually developing autonomy in each region of the world, became the communion as it exists today.

## Origins

![https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/22/DublinStPatricksCathedral_adjusted.JPG/250px-DublinStPatricksCathedral_adjusted.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/22/DublinStPatricksCathedral_adjusted.JPG/250px-DublinStPatricksCathedral_adjusted.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail "SHA-256: 22a337be62f10707d4eb7ca6e385eb860ef46d70fc7e3cf6c981ba642dfeed46")

St Patrick's Cathedral, Dublin in Dublin.

The only [provinces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecclesiastical_province "Ecclesiastical province") of the [Anglican Communion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglican_Communion "Anglican Communion") with a direct and unbroken history stretching back to the pre-Reformation church are to be found in [Great Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain "Great Britain") and [Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ireland "Ireland"): the [Church of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England"), the [Church in Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_in_Wales "Church in Wales"), the [Church of Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_Ireland "Church of Ireland") and the [Scottish Episcopal Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_Episcopal_Church "Scottish Episcopal Church"). As its name suggests, the Scottish situation is unique; the national [Church of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_Scotland "Church of Scotland") is [Presbyterian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterian "Presbyterian") and for some years in the late 17th and early 18th centuries the Scottish Episcopal Church, despite its similarities to the Church of England, was regarded with some suspicion because of its occasional associations with [Jacobite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobitism "Jacobitism") opposition to the [House of Hanover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Hanover "House of Hanover").

Although [Henry VIII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_VIII_of_England "Henry VIII of England") broke with the [Church of Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Papacy "Papacy") in the 1530s, he strongly resisted thereafter associating the English Church with the Continental Protestant Reformation. [^1] Henry's position was however, reversed in the brief reign of his young son [Edward VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_VI "Edward VI") 1547–1553, when the leaders of the Church of England, especially [Thomas Cranmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Cranmer "Thomas Cranmer"), actively sought to establish England in the centre of evolving [Reformed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reformed_tradition "Reformed tradition") churches.[^2] Cranmer's ambitions, however, were not widely shared amongst the bulk of laity and clergy; and accordingly, the return to the religious forms of traditional Roman Catholicism under [Queen Mary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_I_of_England "Mary I of England") was widely welcomed.

The [Elizabethan Settlement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabethan_Settlement "Elizabethan Settlement") in England was broken in 1570 with the [excommunication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Excommunication "Excommunication") of Elizabeth.[^3] Although few, if any, concessions were made to the Papacy or to Roman Catholic doctrine, a small number of changes were then made to the Articles of Religion and to the Prayer Book, especially in relation the [Real Presence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Presence "Real Presence") and to the continuation of worship in more traditional forms.[^4] Only one of Mary's English and Welsh bishops conformed to the Elizabethan settlement, though all save 300 of the parish clergy subscribed. In [Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ireland "Ireland") the position was reversed; all bishops save two accepted the Elizabethan Settlement, but the bulk of parish clergy and laity remained loyal to the pope. In the period since 1553, [Continental Reformed Protestantism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continental_Reformed_Protestantism "Continental Reformed Protestantism") had itself continued to develop, especially in [Geneva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geneva "Geneva") and [Heidelberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heidelberg "Heidelberg"), but English divines who wished the Elizabethan church to take part in these developments were to be bitterly disappointed; Elizabeth refused any further change to the forms or structures of religion established in 1559.[^5] In particular, Protestant controversialists began to attack the [episcopal polity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Episcopal_polity "Episcopal polity"), and the defined [liturgy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liturgy "Liturgy") of the Elizabethan Church as incompatible with the true Reformed tradition; and, in response, defenders of the established church began, from the early 17th Century onwards, to claim these specific features as positively desirable, or indeed essential.[^6]

The attempt to impose in Scotland a Prayer Book on the English model, drove the three kingdoms into [civil war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Civil_War "English Civil War"). However, the Puritan sympathies of the victorious Parliamentary armies in the English Civil War, and the consequential abolition during the [Commonwealth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_of_England "Commonwealth of England") of English bishoprics and cathedral chapters with the suppression of the Book of Common Prayer, resulted in English churchmen beginning to recognise Anglican identity as being distinct from and incompatible with the traditions of [Presbyterian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterian "Presbyterian") Protestantism. This distinction was formalised at the [Restoration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Restoration "English Restoration") of [Charles II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_II_of_England "Charles II of England"), when the proposals of Puritan divines for further reform of the Prayer Book were thoroughly rejected; and 1,760 clergymen were deprived of their livings for failing to subscribe to the 1662 Book. From this date onwards [dissenting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dissenting "Dissenting") Protestant congregations were to be found throughout England, and the established church no longer claimed or sought to comprehend all traditions of Protestant belief. In [Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ireland "Ireland") and in many of England's American Colonies, the numbers who subscribed to Presbyterian congregations formed the majority of the Protestant population; while in Scotland from 1689, following the [accession of William and Mary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glorious_Revolution "Glorious Revolution"), Presbyterian church polity was revived, and constituted in that kingdom, the established church; so that those ministers and congregations who continued to subscribe to the Anglican Episcopalian traditions eventually became a dissenting minority.

In the 18th and 19th centuries, divines of the Church of England increasingly differentiated their faith from that of the Protestant churches. items.body_excerpt:
**Anglican doctrine** (also called **Episcopal doctrine** in some countries) is the body of Christian teachings used to guide the religious and moral practices of [Anglicanism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglicanism "Anglicanism").[^6]

[Thomas Cranmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Cranmer "Thomas Cranmer"), the guiding Reformer that led to the development of Anglicanism as a distinct tradition under the [English Reformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Reformation "English Reformation"), compiled the original *[Book of Common Prayer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Book_of_Common_Prayer "Book of Common Prayer")*, which forms the basis of Anglican worship and practice.[^7] [^6] By 1571 it included the [Thirty-nine Articles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thirty-nine_Articles "Thirty-nine Articles"), the historic doctrinal statement of the [Church of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England").[^6] *[The Books of Homilies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Books_of_Homilies "The Books of Homilies")* explicates the foundational teachings of Anglican Christianity, also compiled under the auspices of Archbishop Cranmer.[^6] [Richard Hooker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Hooker "Richard Hooker") and the [Caroline divines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caroline_divines "Caroline divines") later developed Anglican doctrine of religious authority as being derived from scripture, tradition, and "redeemed" reason; Anglicans affirmed the *primacy* of scriptural revelation ([prima scriptura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prima_scriptura "Prima scriptura")), informed by the [Church Fathers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_Fathers "Church Fathers"), the historic [Nicene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicene_Creed "Nicene Creed"), [Apostles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apostles'_Creed "Apostles' Creed") and [Athanasian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athanasian_Creed "Athanasian Creed") creeds, and a latitudinarian interpretation of [scholasticism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scholasticism "Scholasticism"). [Charles Simeon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Simeon "Charles Simeon") espoused and popularised evangelical [Reformed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reformed_Christianity "Reformed Christianity") positions in the 18th and 19th centuries, while the [Oxford Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxford_Movement "Oxford Movement") re-introduced [monasticism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_monasticism "Christian monasticism"), [religious orders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglican_religious_orders "Anglican religious orders") and various other pre-Reformation practices and beliefs in the 19th century.

Anglicanism historically developed as *[via media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Via_media#Anglicanism "Via media")* between two branches of Protestantism— [Lutheranism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lutheranism "Lutheranism") and [Calvinism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calvinism "Calvinism") —though closer to the latter than the former.[^8] [^9] Its identity has affirmed to be [Reformed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reformed_Christianity "Reformed Christianity") and [Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_\(term\) "Catholic (term)").[^8]

Over time, the tension between [catholicity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholicity "Catholicity") and [Puritanism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puritans "Puritans") resulted in a [latitudinarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latitudinarian "Latitudinarian") or " [broad church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broad_church "Broad church") " mainstream, within a [low church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low_church "Low church") to [high church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_church "High church") spectrum of sanctioned approaches to ritual and tolerance of the associated beliefs. [Evangelicals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evangelical_Anglicanism "Evangelical Anglicanism") (low church) and [Anglo Catholics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo_Catholics "Anglo Catholics") (high church) represent the far ends of this spectrum, with most Anglicans falling somewhere in [between](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_churchmanship "Central churchmanship"). Theologically, the Anglican Communion includes [Reformed Anglicanism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reformed_Anglicanism "Reformed Anglicanism"), with a smaller number of [Arminian Anglicans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglican_Arminianism "Anglican Arminianism").[^10]

## Approach to doctrine

There are two streams informing doctrinal development and understanding in Anglicanism. The first of these includes the historic formularies of Anglicanism.[^9] Historical formularies of Anglicanism include [*Books of Common Prayer*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Book_of_Common_Prayer "Book of Common Prayer"), [ordinals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordinal_\(liturgy\) "Ordinal (liturgy)") and the "standard divines". Most prominent of the historical formularies are the [Thirty-Nine Articles of Religion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thirty-Nine_Articles_of_Religion "Thirty-Nine Articles of Religion"), principally authored by [Thomas Cranmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Cranmer "Thomas Cranmer").[^6] These are divided into four sections, moving from the general (the fundamentals of the faith) to the particular (the interpretation of scripture, the structure and authority of the church, and the relationship between church and society). Other significant formularies include [The Books of Homilies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Books_of_Homilies "The Books of Homilies"), listed in Article XXXV in the Articles of Religion; this explicates the theology of historic Anglicanism.[^6]

Some Anglicans also take the principle of *[lex orandi, lex credendi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lex_orandi,_lex_credendi "Lex orandi, lex credendi")* seriously, regarding the content, form and rubrics of [liturgy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liturgy "Liturgy") as an important element of doctrinal understanding, development and interpretation. Secondly, Anglicans cite the work of the standard divines, or foundational theologians, of Anglicanism as instructive. Such divines include [Cranmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Cranmer "Thomas Cranmer"), [Richard Hooker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Hooker "Richard Hooker"), [Matthew Parker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matthew_Parker "Matthew Parker"), [John Ponet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Ponet "John Ponet"), [Lancelot Andrewes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancelot_Andrewes "Lancelot Andrewes") and [John Jewel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Jewel "John Jewel").

Anglican doctrine affirms the three major creeds of the early [ecumenical councils](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecumenical_council "Ecumenical council") (the [Apostles'](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apostles'_Creed "Apostles' Creed"), [Nicene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicene_Creed "Nicene Creed") and [Athanasian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athanasian_Creed "Athanasian Creed") creeds), the principles enshrined in the " [Chicago-Lambeth Quadrilateral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago-Lambeth_Quadrilateral "Chicago-Lambeth Quadrilateral") " and the dispersed authority of the four [instruments of Communion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglican_Communion#Instruments_of_communion "Anglican Communion") of the [Anglican Communion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglican_Communion "Anglican Communion").

The second stream of doctrine is contained in the formally adopted doctrinal positions of the constitutions and [canon law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canon_law "Canon law") of various national churches and provinces of the Anglican Communion. These are usually formulated by [general synods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_synod "General synod") of national or regional churches and interpreted and enforced by a [bishop](https://en.wikipedia

items.body_excerpt:
The **Anglican realignment** is a movement among some [Anglicans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglican "Anglican") to align themselves under new or alternative oversight within or outside the [Anglican Communion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglican_Communion "Anglican Communion").

Two of the major events that contributed to the movement were the 2002 decision of the [Diocese of New Westminster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglican_Diocese_of_New_Westminster "Anglican Diocese of New Westminster") in Canada to authorise a rite of blessing for [same-sex unions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Same-sex_union "Same-sex union"), and the nomination of two openly gay priests in 2003 to become bishops. [Jeffrey John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeffrey_John "Jeffrey John"), an openly gay priest with a long-time partner, was appointed to be the next [Bishop of Reading](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop_of_Reading "Bishop of Reading") in the [Church of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England") and the [General Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Convention "General Convention") of the Episcopal Church ratified the election of [Gene Robinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gene_Robinson "Gene Robinson"), an openly gay non-celibate man,[^1] as [Bishop of New Hampshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Episcopal_Diocese_of_New_Hampshire "Episcopal Diocese of New Hampshire").[^2] Jeffrey John ultimately declined the appointment due to pressure.[^3]

The current realignment movement differs from previous ones in that on the one hand some Anglicans are seeking to establish different [ecclesiastical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecclesiology "Ecclesiology") arrangements within the Anglican Communion rather than separating themselves from it, and on another hand other Anglicans that had previously separated are being gathered into the new realignment structures along with those who were never Anglican/Episcopalian before. Some Anglican [provinces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecclesiastical_province "Ecclesiastical province"), particularly in [Nigeria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_Nigeria "Church of Nigeria"), [Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglican_Church_of_Kenya "Anglican Church of Kenya"), [West Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_the_Province_of_West_Africa "Church of the Province of West Africa"), and [South America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglican_Church_of_South_America "Anglican Church of South America"), are seeking to accommodate them.[^4] A number of parishes that are part of the realignment have severed ties with the Episcopal Church and the Anglican Church of Canada and associated themselves with bishops from these other national Anglican provinces.

The conventions of four dioceses of the Episcopal Church voted in 2007 and 2008 to leave that church and to join the Anglican Church of South America. Twelve other jurisdictions, serving an estimated 100,000 persons at that time, formed on December 3–4, 2008 a [Confessing Anglican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confessing_Anglican "Confessing Anglican") body, the [Anglican Church in North America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglican_Church_in_North_America "Anglican Church in North America") (ACNA). The ACNA is seeking official recognition as a province within the Anglican Communion.[^5] The Church of Nigeria declared itself in communion with the new church in March 2009 and the [Global Fellowship of Confessing Anglicans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_Fellowship_of_Confessing_Anglicans "Global Fellowship of Confessing Anglicans") (GAFCON) formally recognized the new church in April 2009.[^6] [^7] In June 2009, the [Anglican Church of Uganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_Uganda "Church of Uganda") also declared itself in full communion with the ACNA, and the [Anglican Church of Sudan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Episcopal_Church_of_Sudan "Episcopal Church of Sudan") followed suit in December 2011.[^8] [^9]

In October 2025, GAFCON Chairman [Laurent Mbanda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurent_Mbanda "Laurent Mbanda"), the Primate of Rwanda, announced that the GAFCON communion will officially be renamed the Global Anglican Communion and was planning to select a new *[primus inter pares](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primus_inter_pares "Primus inter pares")* instead of the Archbishop of Canterbury. He also asserted that GAFCON is not leaving the Anglican Communion but rather is the Anglican Communion.[^10] The election was going to take place at the next GAFCON, due to take place in March 2026 in [Abuja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abuja "Abuja"), Nigeria, hosted by the [Church of Nigeria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_Nigeria "Church of Nigeria").[^11] Mbanda said that in the wake of the appointment of [Sarah Mullally](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Mullally "Sarah Mullally") as the [Archbishop of Canterbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archbishop_of_Canterbury "Archbishop of Canterbury"), and the resulting controversy it poses amongst evangelical Anglicans, that "this may be the most significant gathering of faithful Anglicans since 2008." [^12] "The statement outlining that plan was signed by one person, Rwanda Archbishop Laurent Mbanda, who serves as chair of GAFCON’s primate council." [^13] In March, 2026, GAFCON declined to elect a "rival" *primus inter pares*, opting instead to reorganize the existing Primates' Council as the "Global Anglican Council." [^14] [^15]

As of 2025, GAFCON claims to represent upwards of 85% of the world's practicing Anglicans.[^16] [^17] [^18] Peer-reviewed research from 2015 and 2016, published in the *[Journal of Anglican Studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journal_of_Anglican_Studies "Journal of Anglican Studies")* by [Cambridge University Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge_University_Press "Cambridge University Press"), indicates that the GAFCON-aligned provinces represent closer to 45% of practicing Anglicans and just over 54% of all Anglicans.[^19] [^20] Excluding the United churches in South Asia, the [World Christian Database](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Christian_Encyclopedia "World Christian Encyclopedia"), published in 2021 and produced by the Center for the Study of Global Christianity at [Gordon-Conwell Theological Seminary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gordon%E2%80%93Conwell_Theological_Seminary "Gordon–Conwell Theological Seminary"), estimated that the Anglican Communion had 97,399,000 members in 2020 with 63,556,000 in Africa, 24,400,000 in Europe, 4,565,000 in Oceania, 2,689,000 in North America, 1,230,000 in Asia, and 959,000 in Latin America.[^21]

## Overview

The movement that involves secession from local dioceses or provinces and yet seeks to remain within the Anglican Communion has been criticised by opponents who claim that, under historic Anglican polity, such a move is not possible. The concept of alternative episcopal oversight first arose a generation ago with the debate over the [ordination of women](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordination_of_women "Ordination of women"). At that time, the movement manifested itself as an effort to accommodate conservative parishes and dioceses that did not want to accept the authority of women consecrated as bishops or bishops who ordained women, by providing pastoral oversight from a bishop who shared their conservative theology. The most thoroughly developed example of this involved the appointment of [provincial episcopal visitors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provincial_episcopal_visitor "Provincial episcopal visitor") in the [Church of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England"), beginning in 1994, who attend to the pastoral needs of parishes and clergy who do not recognise that [holy orders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglican_ministry "Anglican ministry") can or should be conferred on women. items.body_excerpt:
**Anglicanism**, also known as **Episcopalianism** in some countries,[^6] [^7] is a [Western](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Christianity "Western Christianity") [Christian tradition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_tradition "Christian tradition") which developed from the practices, [liturgy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_liturgy "Christian liturgy") and identity of the [Church of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England") following the [English Reformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Reformation "English Reformation"),[^8] in the context of the [Protestant Reformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestant_Reformation "Protestant Reformation") in Europe. It is one of the largest branches of [Christianity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianity "Christianity"), with around 110 million adherents within the [Anglican Communion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglican_Communion "Anglican Communion"), and approximately 2.4 million outside of the Anglican Communion, worldwide as of 2025.[^9] [^10] [^11] [^12] [^13]

Adherents of Anglicanism are called *Anglicans*; they are also called *Episcopalians* [^14] in some countries. Most are members of national or regional [ecclesiastical provinces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecclesiastical_province#Anglican_Communion "Ecclesiastical province") of the international Anglican Communion,[^15] one of the largest Christian bodies in the world,[^16] and the world's third-largest Christian communion.[^9] [^17] [^18] [^19] [^20] [^21] The provinces within the Anglican Communion have historically been in [full communion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Full_communion "Full communion") with the [See of Canterbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/See_of_Canterbury "See of Canterbury") and thus with the [archbishop of Canterbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archbishop_of_Canterbury "Archbishop of Canterbury"), whom the communion refers to as its *[primus inter pares](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primus_inter_pares#Anglican_Communion "Primus inter pares")* ([Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin "Latin"), 'first among equals'). The archbishop calls the decennial [Lambeth Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lambeth_Conference "Lambeth Conference"), chairs the meeting of [primates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primates_in_the_Anglican_Communion "Primates in the Anglican Communion"), and is the president of the [Anglican Consultative Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglican_Consultative_Council "Anglican Consultative Council").[^22] [^23] Some churches that are not part of the Anglican Communion or recognised by it also call themselves Anglican, including those that are within the [Continuing Anglican movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continuing_Anglican_movement "Continuing Anglican movement") and [Anglican realignment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglican_realignment "Anglican realignment").[^24]

Anglicans base their Christian faith on the [Bible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestant_Bible "Protestant Bible"), traditions of the apostolic church, [apostolic succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apostolic_succession "Apostolic succession") (" [historic episcopate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historic_episcopate_\(Anglican_views\) "Historic episcopate (Anglican views)") "), and the writings of the [Church Fathers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_Fathers "Church Fathers"), as well as, historically, the *[Thirty-nine Articles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thirty-nine_Articles "Thirty-nine Articles")* and *[The Books of Homilies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Books_of_Homilies "The Books of Homilies")*.[^25] [^8]

Anglicanism forms a branch of [Western Christianity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Christianity "Western Christianity"), having declared its independence from the [Holy See](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_See "Holy See") through the [Act of Supremacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acts_of_Supremacy "Acts of Supremacy") in 1534, a separation later consolidated by the [Elizabethan Religious Settlement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabethan_Religious_Settlement "Elizabethan Religious Settlement"). Many of the Anglican formularies of the mid-16th century correspond closely to those of historical [Protestantism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestantism "Protestantism").[^26] In the first half of the 17th century, the Church of England and the associated [Church of Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_Ireland "Church of Ireland") were presented by some Anglican divines as comprising a distinct Christian tradition, with theologies, structures, and forms of worship representing a different kind of middle way, or *[via media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Via_media "Via media")*, originally between Lutheranism and Calvinism,[^27] [^28] and later between Protestantism and Catholicism – a perspective that came to be highly influential in later theories of Anglican identity and expressed in the description of Anglicanism as "catholic and reformed".[^29] The degree of distinction between Protestant and Catholic tendencies within Anglicanism is routinely a matter of debate both within specific Anglican churches and the Anglican Communion. The *[Book of Common Prayer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Book_of_Common_Prayer "Book of Common Prayer")* is unique to Anglicanism, the collection of services in one prayer book used for centuries. The book is acknowledged as a principal tie that binds the Anglican Communion as a liturgical tradition.[^25]

After the [American Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Revolution "American Revolution"), Anglican congregations in the United States and [British North America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_North_America "British North America") (which would later form the basis for the modern country of Canada) were each reconstituted into autonomous churches with their own bishops and self-governing structures; these were known as the [Protestant Episcopal Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Episcopal_Church_\(United_States\) "Episcopal Church (United States)") in the United States and the [Church of England in the Dominion of Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglican_Church_of_Canada "Anglican Church of Canada"). Through the expansion of the [British Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Empire "British Empire") and the activity of [Christian missions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_mission "Christian mission"), this model was adopted as the model for many newly formed churches, especially in Africa, [Australasia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australasia "Australasia"), and the Asia-Pacific. In the late-19th century, the term *Anglicanism* was coined to describe the common religious tradition of these churches and also that of the [Scottish Episcopal Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_Episcopal_Church "Scottish Episcopal Church"), which, though originating earlier within the [Church of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_Scotland "Church of Scotland"), had come to be recognised as sharing this common identity. By the 21st century, the global centre of Anglicanism had shifted to the [Global South](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_South "Global South"), particularly sub-Saharan Africa, with 63,556,000 in Africa, 24,400,000 in Europe, 4,565,000 in Oceania, 2,689,000 in Northern America, 1,230,000 in Asia, and 959,000 in Latin America in 2020.[^30] [^31]

![https://web.archive.org/web/20180817210534im_/http://strivepsychology.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/05/SigLogo.png](https://web.archive.org/web/20180817210534im_/http://strivepsychology.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/05/SigLogo.png "SHA-256: 3b9fd457c057f7e20d9bac0476b85e0aa034abfbdc3b79255629f0c1e8a53958")

## A Simple Mission

Dr. John Matthias has a simple mission – to facilitate self-discovery to make a difference in the world, whether this involves helping clients to overcome past traumas or to become exceptional leaders or parents. He has primarily worked as a [clinical psychologist](https://web.archive.org/web/20180817210534/http://www.apa.org/ed/graduate/specialize/clinical.aspx) and as an organizational consultant with a focus upon leadership for several major organizations, including the [Andre Agassi Foundation](https://web.archive.org/web/20180817210534/http://www.agassifoundation.org/). He has been fortunate to have had several exceptional mentors, including the pioneering psychologist Rodney Goodyear and the leadership guru [Warren Bennis](https://web.archive.org/web/20180817210534/http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Bennis) while receiving his doctorate from the University of Southern California. Dr. Matthias also graduated with honors in philosophy from Princeton University under the guidance of the renowned philosopher, [Gilbert Harman](https://web.archive.org/web/20180817210534/http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilbert_Harman). He won the prestigious McCosh Thesis prize at Princeton University. He was an All-Chicago and All-State football player in high school and he played college football at Princeton. He was also high school valedictorian at a large public high school in Chicago where he was chosen for a valedictory study that continues to this day.

![https://web.archive.org/web/20180817210534im_/http://strivepsychology.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/04/BanksFeminist.jpg](https://web.archive.org/web/20180817210534im_/http://strivepsychology.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/04/BanksFeminist.jpg "SHA-256: 1a1f48113891928b14a6b18a908b2987fbb618c792871d5aac1ab072addf4885")

Dr. Matthias has acquired an enormous depth and breath of psychological knowledge over his twenty year career as a psychologist, including in the domains of forensic, clinical, family and [organizational psychology](https://web.archive.org/web/20180817210534/http://www.apa.org/ed/graduate/specialize/industrial.aspx). In the forensic context he has assessed hundreds of high risk felons for community placement, developing expertise in personality assessments and hidden behavioral motivations. In the clinical realm he has worked with numerous victims of abuse and trauma, including with survivors of the recent Las Vegas shooting massacre and 9/11. As a family therapist Dr. Matthias received his Master’s degree in Marriage, Family and Child counseling and he has worked with hundreds of families, couples and children over the years. He still supervises UNLV doctoral students on play therapy and family systems. As an organizational consultant he has worked with many community leaders and CEO’s, assisting them to achieve insight and excellence in their domains. He has also worked with several organizations seeking transformation by applying a unique research model he developed drawing parallels between the qualities of exceptional teams and exceptional families. By working with individuals and groups across such a wide spectrum of areas that have included both deficits and strengths, Dr. Matthias has developed a keen understanding of human beings at their highest and lowest points across the entire spectrum of human psychological development and functioning, which has led to greater wisdom about the major ingredients necessary for mastery and the development of resiliency and psychological well-being.

## Challenged by Warren Bennis

to develop a grand unified theory of leadership many years ago, Dr. Matthias has become increasingly interested in the impact of exceptional leadership and the ability of strong leaders to leave a mark on the world. He has also explored the elements of mastery across many domains, including therapy and personality assessment. Toward that end, he has trained numerous doctoral students in clinical psychology at UNLV- many of whom have gone onto leadership positions in their organizations. He has also worked with leaders in many domains, including sports, health care, and business, to assist them in broadening their influence and he has helped many individuals on their paths towards mastery. He has been guided by the persistent questions: What makes an exceptional leader? And are there any common elements for leadership and mastery across domains? He is currently writing two books addressing these questions. The first book, *Strive: The New Psychology of Meaning and Mastery*, will be published in 2019. The second book, *Leading Lives: Wednesdays with Warren Bennis and the Search for a Grand Unified Theory of Leadership*, will be published in 2020. He also recently started a podcast- Strive- to assist people in striving for meaning and mastery through conversations with remarkable people and academics who share their ideas, research and stories about their personal journeys to strive for meaning and mastery in their daily lives and work with the goal of helping others to do the same.

![https://web.archive.org/web/20180817210534im_/http://strivepsychology.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/04/Banks-at-SnowCanyon.jpg](https://web.archive.org/web/20180817210534im_/http://strivepsychology.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/04/Banks-at-SnowCanyon.jpg "SHA-256: 09c9b63c95cd81acdf32c0f62575617ed3ab00dda0cd1493ab7975d932343d9d")

## PROJECTS iHOPE & iSTRIVE

Dr. Matthias recently launched two initiatives- Project iHope, which provides adventure experiences for children with terminal illnesses and their families, and Project iStrive, which provides a platform for individuals to share their most passionate strivings for the future.

Dr. Matthias is a licensed psychologist in both Utah and Nevada. He is an adjunct faculty member at the University of Nevada Las Vegas in the clinical psychology doctoral program. He is also a certified Eagala mental health specialist and he often incorporates equine work into his adventure experiences. He is an avid canyoneer and he gains sustenance and energy from the beautiful canyons of Southern Utah. As a new father of a beautiful baby boy, Dr. John holds out hope for a future worth inhabiting. His personal mission is to strive for love, peace, wisdom, kindness, knowledge and service to others.

[![](https://web.archive.org/web/20180817210534im_/http://strivepsychology.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/04/Banks_In-Arms.jpg)](https://web.archive.org/web/20180817210534/http://strivepsychology.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/04/Banks_In-Arms.jpg)

### In PraiseOf all thingsWild

You can learn more about Dr. Matthias from his abbreviated autobiographical blog post, **In Praise of All Things Wild**.
